issues.title: The accessible name (from the link’s text), together with the absence of programmatically determined link context, does not describe the purpose of the link.
issues.why_it_matters_for_persona: As an autistic person, ambiguous links like 'More' are a significant source of anxiety and cognitive friction. I need to know exactly where a link will take me before I click it to maintain a predictable browsing experience. When I see a generic link, I have to stop and read the surrounding text to figure out its purpose, which breaks my concentration and adds unnecessary mental effort.
remediation_instructions: The best practice is to use a native `` element with a descriptive `href` attribute instead of a `div` with a link role. For example: `More about the main content`.

If you must use a `div`, provide a more descriptive accessible name. You can change the text content: `
More about the main content
`.

Alternatively, add an `aria-label` to the `div`: `
More
`.
Additionally, ensure the element is keyboard accessible by adding a JavaScript `keydown` event listener that triggers the `click` action when the Enter key is pressed.
expected_tool_change: An automated accessibility checker will flag the ambiguous accessible name 'More'. It may also flag the use of a non-interactive element as a link.
A screen reader currently announces 'More, link'. After fixing, it will announce the full descriptive name, such as 'More about the main content, link'.
